subsection: 2. Costs and revenue streams: fixed, variable and recurring income

notes.b: Costs are classified by how they behave as output changes. Each cost belongs to one group, so learn the test for each.
points: Fixed costs stay the same in total whatever the level of output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and the salaries of permanent staff.
Variable costs change directly with output, such as raw materials, packaging and wages paid per item made.
Electricity is semi-variable, because it has a fixed standing charge as well as a charge that rises with usage.
Total cost equals fixed costs plus variable costs at a given level of output.

notes.b: Costs can also be grouped by when they arise in the life of the business.
points: Start-up costs are incurred before trading begins, such as legal fees, fit-out of premises, equipment and initial stock.
Running costs are the ongoing costs of operating once trading starts, such as wages, rent, utilities and marketing.
Start-up costs are usually one-off, so they weigh heavily on cash in the early months.
A business that underestimates its running costs can run short of cash even when sales are growing.

notes.b: A revenue stream is a source of income. The main difference between streams is how often the customer pays.
points: A one-off transaction is a single sale where the customer pays once, such as buying a laptop or a meal in a restaurant.
A recurring stream brings in income repeatedly, which makes cash flow easier to predict.
A subscription is a regular fee for continued access to a product or service, such as a monthly gym membership.
Licensing earns fees for letting others use intellectual property such as a brand, patent or software.
Usage fees charge customers according to how much they use a service, such as a per-unit charge for mobile data.
Advertising revenue comes from selling space or airtime to other businesses, which is how many free apps and websites earn their income.

notes.b: Profit is what remains when costs are deducted from revenue. Break-even is the output at which total revenue equals total cost.
points: Profit equals total revenue minus total costs.
Contribution per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit, and it goes towards covering fixed costs.
Break-even quantity equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit.
Sample figures: fixed costs of €6,000, a selling price of €15 and a variable cost of €9 give a contribution of €6 and a break-even of 1,000 units.
Above break-even each extra unit adds to profit, while below it the business makes a loss.

notes.b: Costs and revenues change as a product, and the business as a whole, moves through its life cycle.
points: In the introduction stage sales are low, promotion costs are high and the business may make a loss.
In the growth stage sales rise quickly and unit costs fall as output increases, so profit grows.
In the maturity stage sales level off, competition increases and price pressure reduces margins.
In the decline stage sales fall, so the business may cut costs, narrow its range or withdraw the product.
Over the business life cycle the mix of costs and revenue streams shifts too, and a mature firm may rely more on recurring income.

notes.b: The mix of costs and revenue streams affects a business's risk as well as its profit.
points: A business dependent on one-off sales has less predictable cash flow than one with recurring income.
High fixed costs make profit sensitive to changes in sales, so a small fall in sales can turn a profit into a loss.
Moving to subscriptions can build customer loyalty, but customers may cancel if the service stops providing value.

questions.prompt: A café owner is opening a coffee shop in Galway. Classify the main costs as fixed, variable or semi-variable, distinguish start-up costs from running costs, and explain how costs and revenue would change as the shop moves through the business life cycle.
questions.model: Classification: rent, insurance and permanent staff salaries are fixed; coffee beans, milk, cups and packaging are variable; electricity is semi-variable. Start-up: the espresso machine, fit-out, licences, legal fees and initial stock, all paid before the first sale. Running: rent, utilities, staff wages and marketing that continue once trading starts. Revenue: mainly one-off sales of coffee, which could be supplemented by recurring income from a loyalty subscription or regular sales of bags of beans. Life cycle: in the introduction stage marketing spend is high and sales low, so a loss is likely; in the growth stage sales rise and unit costs fall; in the maturity stage competition squeezes prices, so the owner must control costs closely.

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of €10,000, a selling price of €20 per unit and a variable cost of €12 per unit. Calculate its break-even quantity and explain what happens to profit above that level of output.
questions.model: Contribution per unit is €20 minus €12, which is €8. Break-even quantity is €10,000 divided by €8, which is 1,250 units. Above 1,250 units each additional unit adds €8 to profit, because the contribution covers the unit's own variable cost and the fixed costs have already been covered.
